shots.text: Triangular eyes, the pupils pierced right through.
shots.credit: Nok terracotta head · Honolulu Museum of Art (8349.1) · Photo: Hiart, CC0

shots.text: Above them, an elaborate hairstyle, worked in fired clay.
shots.credit: Nok terracotta head · Honolulu Museum of Art (8349.1) · Photo: Hiart, CC0

shots.text: The style is called Nok, after a culture of central Nigeria.
shots.desc: wooded plateau of central Nigeria at first light, granite outcrops, mist in valleys

shots.text: Its excavators describe Nok as the earliest large-scale sculptural tradition in sub-Saharan Africa.
shots.desc: excavation trench edge at dawn, trowel and brush on red earth

shots.text: Yet they found no evidence of a state, of towns, or of an elite.
shots.desc: open savanna woodland, no buildings, long shadows

shots.text: So could small, scattered farming communities have made art on this scale?
shots.desc: a lone thatched homestead far off across a millet field at dusk

shots.text: The first of these terracottas was noticed in 1928, during tin mining at the village of Nok.
The British archaeologist Bernard Fagg collected the finds, and gave them a name: the Nok culture.
shots.desc: generic mid-century archive shelves with closed boxes, soft window light, no desk, no person, no papers with writing

shots.text: Many of his pieces came from tin-mine gravels, moved from where they had first lain.
shots.desc: wet alluvial gravels in an old tin-mine cutting, overcast
